bearings.paper_claim: Within the same MP (MP fixed effects), PMQ speeches score 1.562 to 1.663 points higher on the emotive-minus-neutral scale than other debates (Table 3 Models 3-5; speech-level SD 8.95; UK 2001-2019, 958,925 speeches). The Queen's Speech opening day is 2.064 in Model 5. The authors read this as a venue pattern and say it is not causally identified.
bearings.paper_location: Table 3 p. 8 with Models 3-5 on p. 9; SD on p. 7; causal caveat p. 10
bearings.system_side: The default corpus pools social posts, CREC floor speech and INTERVIEW turns per member into one text list (CHRG excluded by default). Per-member category rates are per-1000-word. Genre is only a validation hook (BIG5_SOURCES), not a covariate, so members with different venue mixes can differ in affect rates for venue reasons.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/big5_traits.py:36-73 (corpus pooling and BIG5_SOURCES hook); fec/members/big5_traits.py:220 (per-1000-word rates); fec/members/big5_traits.py:179-182 (posemo/negemo weights in E, ES, A, C)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies only if US floor speech, interviews and social posts differ in audience exposure the way PMQs differs from ordinary Commons debate. The paper covers UK and Irish lower houses with a valence-agnostic ANEW-based score, not LIWC posemo/negemo. The speech-level shift is about 0.18 SD. Observational, not causal.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers verified in Table 3 (2.226, 1.562, 1.618, 1.663, 2.064). Dropped the claim that venue, not speaker, shifts word rates: the paper says the design cannot causally identify audience effects, so the bearing states only that the gap persists within MP. Code line range corrected: E weights sit at line 179, not 180-183. The z-scoring step was not re-read in this pass.

bearings.paper_claim: The authors argue, without causal identification, that legislators raise emotive rhetoric when addressing voters: PMQ speeches are higher within the same MP (about +1.6, Table 3) and Irish Leaders' Questions higher by +2.5 to +4.6 (Table 5, N=945,734). The paper does not test whether speakers keep their rank order in affect across venues.
bearings.paper_location: Theory pp. 3-4; Table 3 p. 8; Table 5 p. 12; causal caveat p. 10
bearings.system_side: affective_n is built from INTERVIEW turns only (source filter in emit_affective_n.py), and the recorded transfer of interview N to floor and hearing text failed. The paper gives a plausible venue mechanism for that failure. The rho values cited in the item (.050, .161) were not found in the cited code or in fec/members text files checked in this pass.

bearings.transfer_conditions: Explains, does not prove, the transfer failure. The paper tests average venue shifts, not member rank-order preservation, which is what rho measures. Does not license re-scoring floor text.
bearings.verifier_note: Ireland range 2.5 to 4.6 verified in Table 5. The text pass cannot tell which Table 5 columns carry MP fixed effects, so 'the same legislators' is not established for Ireland and was removed. The rho values could not be traced to any file and are left unverified.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotiveness is measured valence-agnostically: percent emotive words (ANEW, 851 emotive seeds) minus percent neutral words (970 neutral seeds). Skip-gram embeddings expand the dictionary to 2,015 emotive and 2,095 neutral UK words, following Rice and Zorn (2019). Scale runs from -100 to +100; mean 0.88, SD 8.95.
bearings.paper_location: Measurement section pp. 5-7 (Equation 1; dictionary counts p. 6; scale and SD p. 7)
bearings.system_side: Live press intensity is abs(lsd_net_norm), i.e. abs(pos - neg)/words, chosen by the CU_S5_INTENSITY default of net_norm. stage5_lsd.R also emits lsd_charge = (pos + neg)/words, used only when INTENSITY is charge. The LSD tone dictionary is generic with no domain expansion (not re-verified in this pass).

bearings.paper_claim: Hypothesis H (p. 4): legislators use more emotive rhetoric in high-profile debates with a larger general audience. The theory section adds that overt emotion can signal weak credibility, so speakers balance ethos, logos and pathos by audience. The paper studies parliamentary speech only, not press releases.
bearings.paper_location: Hypothesis p. 4; theory pp. 3-4; conclusion pp. 12-13
bearings.system_side: press_value = stance sign x heat, where heat defaults to abs(lsd_net_norm) (run_stage5.R:141-143). press_matrix in moneyball_core.py normalizes signed extrema within each domain. Press releases are one public-facing venue, so the intensity term may index messaging style more than commitment; this is analyst inference, not a paper finding.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only to the extent that between-member intensity differences reflect style rather than commitment. The paper shows within-speaker venue shifts in parliament, not between-member style differences within one venue.
bearings.verifier_note: The original line 'Politicians are most emotive when addressing voters' paraphrases H and the conclusion too strongly; reworded to the text. Hypothesis H location and the credibility trade-off verified. The claim that press-release intensity indexes audience performance is the analyst's extension and is now labeled as such.

summary_issues: The summary says the paper 'supports Paul's ask for venue-specific frameworks' and that 'his note is not stale'. The item has paul_entries empty and no annotation, so this Paul attribution is unsupported here and should be removed or sourced.
The summary's statement that the interview-to-floor N transfer failed (rho .050, .161) has no traceable source in the cited code or fec/members text files checked; unverified.
The summary's statement that venue, not speaker, shifts emotive word rates overstates the paper, which says the design cannot causally identify audience effects (p. 10).
The summary and bearings place the electoral-cycle and causal-caveat text on p. 10; in the extracted text the running-head page numbers are ambiguous, so the page cite is approximate.
Appendices A-J are not in the extracted text; robustness claims that cite them (LIWC, alternative scalings, human validation) are unverified.
Four of the seven related links (Ramey, Aroyehun, Haselmayer, Koutsoumpis) are not cited by this paper; they are analyst judgements between vault items and are kept but labeled.
Abstract reports two million speeches; body analysed samples are 958,925 UK and 945,734 Irish. The summary uses the body figures correctly.
